newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Supermarkets set to shake up South African banking.
newsitem.headline: Supermarkets set to shake up South African banking.

text.p: South Africa's financial services market is bracing for a major shake-up later this year as supermarket giants Pick 'n Pay and Shoprite-Checkers move into in-store banking.
Fairly common in Britain, the concept is new in South Africa and has ruffled feathers in the conservative banking community.

The first supermarket to move into the fray will be Pick 'n Pay, which has contracted Boland Bank to help it run in-store savings schemes. It plans to provide other financial services such as unit trusts and insurance later.
Cape-based Boland Bank has been small fry in the market but is due to become part of the country's fifth largest banking group at the end of April when it delists and merges with NBS.
Some analysts are sceptical about how quickly South Africans will adapt to buying unit trusts or insurance policies while out getting their groceries.
"In-store banking has yet to prove itself in this country," said one analyst.
The banking sector is particularly irked by the fact that Pick 'n Pay does not expect to register as a bank and will therefore not be subject to the same scrutiny as banks.
The Banks Act stipulates that only registered banks can take deposits. But Pick 'n Pay argues that it will only be taking deposits on behalf of Boland Bank, which will administer the accounts.
The Council of South African Banks argues it should still have to register.
Registrar of Banks Christo Wiese said that if Pick 'n Pay was merely facilitating the payment of deposits and withdrawals, registration might not be needed.
To cap it all, Pick 'n Pay is promising better interest rates and services than banks, with their high overheads, are able to offer.
Financial transactions are not completely new to Pick 'n Pay. Consumers can already pay their telephone and municipal services bills, and draw money at its tills.
But problems which could be encountered include maintaining liquidity and increased congestion at the tills as more transactions are undertaken.
"What will they do on a Thursday afternoon before Easter and a few thousand people want to draw 200 rand?" one analyst asked.
Pick 'n Pay group enterprises managing director Gareth Ackerman relishes the prospect.

"The stores themselves take an enormous amount of money, especially at month-end and, quite frankly, from our point of view, the less money that is left in the tills at the end of the day, the better it is for us," he said.
Because its technology would be used to process the transactions, Pick 'n Pay would get a fee for money paid out.
Ackerman admitted that the banks were not happy by this move onto their turf, but said that Pick 'n Pay did not envisage taking a major share of their traditional market.

"I think that the banks have to worry about it in the sense that they will have egg on their faces because we will come in with superior interest rates, lower costs and people will question their own banks," he said.
"But in terms of market share profitability I can't think that we will make a difference."
